Unlike local extrema, absolute extrema are found by comparing the function's values at critical points and the endpoints of the interval. • Step 1: Find all critical points of fff in the interval (a,b)(a, b)(a,b) by solving f′(x)=0f'(x) = 0f′(x)=0 or finding where f′(x)f'(x)f′(x) does not exist. • Step 2: Calculate the value of the function f(x)f(x)f(x) at all the critical points found in Step 1 and at the endpoints x=ax = ax=a and x=bx = bx=b. • Step 3: The largest of these values is the Absolute Maximum value and the smallest is the Absolute Minimum value of fff on [a,b][a, b][a,b]. 📐Formulae f′(x)=0 (Condition for critical points)f'(x) = 0 \text{ (Condition for critical points)}f′(x)=0 (Condition for critical points) Absolute Maximum Value=max⁡{f(a),f(c1),f(c2),…,f(b)}\text{Absolute Maximum Value} = \max{f(a), f(c_1), f(c_2), \dots, f(b)}Absolute Maximum Value=max{f(a),f(c1),f(c2),…,f(b)} Absolute Minimum Value=min⁡{f(a),f(c1),f(c2),…,f(b)}\text{Absolute Minimum Value} = \min{f(a), f(c_1), f(c_2), \dots, f(b)}Absolute Minimum Value=min{f(a),f(c1),f(c2),…,f(b)} For f(x)=ax2+bx+c, critical point is at x=−b2a\text{For } f(x) = ax^2 + bx + c, \text{ critical point is at } x = -\frac{b}{2a}For f(x)=ax2+bx+c, critical point is at x=−2ab 💡Examples Problem 1: Find the absolute maximum and minimum values of the function f(x)=2x3−15x2+36x+1f(x) = 2x^3 - 15x^2 + 36x + 1f(x)=2x3−15x2+36x+1 on the interval [1,5][1, 5][1,5]. Solution: Find the derivative: f′(x)=6x2−30x+36f'(x) = 6x^2 - 30x + 36f′(x)=6x2−30x+36 Set f′(x)=0f'(x) = 0f′(x)=0: 6(x2−5x+6)=0 ⟹ 6(x−2)(x−3)=06(x^2 - 5x + 6) = 0 \implies 6(x - 2)(x - 3) = 06(x2−5x+6)=0⟹6(x−2)(x−3)=0 Thus, critical points are x=2x = 2x=2 and x=3x = 3x=3. content.title: Finding Critical Points — Find critical points of functions of two variables
content.content: Finding Critical Points — Find critical points of functions of two variables Varsity Tutors｡ rely on algebra and linear algebra Applications Surface area, profit with two inputs, physics with two degrees of freedom Machine learning (millions of variables), portfolio optimization, engineering design In machine learning, for example, neural networks have functions with millions of parameters, and training the network is essentially a massive critical-point search. The gradient (the vector of all partial derivatives) is computed, set toward zero, and the system is solved iteratively. The same principle you are learning right now — set every partial derivative to zero — scales up to power the technology behind image recognition, language translation, and much more. SECTION 9 Practice Problems Test your understanding with these five problems, arranged from conceptual understanding through critical thinking. Work through each one on paper before checking the answer. PROBLEM 1 — CONCEPTUAL In your own words, explain why both partial derivatives must equal zero at a critical point of f(x, y). Why isn't it enough for just one of them to be zero? Show Answer PROBLEM 2 — BASIC CALCULATION Find the critical point(s) of f(x, y) = x² + y² − 4x + 6y + 13. Show Answer PROBLEM 3 — INTERMEDIATE Find all critical points of f(x, y) = x³ − 3x + y² − 2y. Show Answer PROBLEM 4 — APPLIED A company's profit P (in thousands of dollars) from producing x units of Product A and y units of Product B is modeled by P(x, y) = −2x² − y² + 12x + 8y − 20. Find the production levels (x, y) that yield critical-point profit, and compute the profit at that point. Show Answer PROBLEM 5 — CRITICAL THINKING Find all critical points of f(x, y) = x² + xy + y² − 6x − 9y. Then explain why the system of equations here is more challenging than in Problem 2 and describe the algebraic strategy you used. Show Answer SUMMARY Lesson Summary To find critical points of a function f(x, y), you compute both partial derivatives — fx (differentiate with respect to x, holding y constant) and fy (differentiate with respect to y, holding x constant) — then set both equal to zero and solve the resulting system of equations simultaneously. Each solution (a, b) is a critical point where the tangent plane is horizontal, making it a candidate for a local maximum, local minimum, or saddle point. The key algebraic challenge varies with the function: if there are no cross-terms (like xy), the two equations decouple and you solve each independently. When cross-terms are present, you must use substitution or elimination to solve the coupled system. Once you've found all critical points, you can classify them using the second derivative test (discriminant D), which is the natural next step in multivariable optimization.

content.content: How to Find the Maximum & Minimum Values of a Function? - Lesson | Study.com Study.com｡ Pay extra attention to the sign of the h value, as it is negative in the standard form of the equation. How to Find the Maximum Value of a Function Let's work through an example to find the maximum value of a function: {eq}f(x) = -3x^2 + 6x + 4 {/eq} Because we are given the equation in the general form, we can find the critical point by first taking the derivative to give us: {eq}f'(x) = -6x + 6 {/eq} Solving for 0 gives us: {eq}0 = -6x + 6 {/eq} {eq}-6 = -6x {/eq} {eq}x = 1 {/eq} This gives us the critical point at x = 1. We can take the second derivative and plug in the critical point to find out if we have a maximum or minimum value. If the second derivative is negative, we will have a maximum. If the second derivative is positive, we will have a minimum. The second derivative test for our example will give us: {eq}f''(x) = -6 {/eq} {eq}f''(1) = -6 {/eq} Since our second derivative is negative, the function has a maximum. We can then plug the critical point back into f(x) to give us the value of our maximum: {eq}f(1) = -3(1)^2 + 6(1) + 4 {/eq} {eq}f(1) = 7 {/eq} This means our maximum will be 7 at the coordinate (1,7). Because this is a quadratic function, this will also be the coordinates for our vertex. We can take a look at the graph of this function: Maximum value at (1,7) How to Find the Minimum Value of a Function Let's do another example to find a minimum value of a function: {eq}f(x) = 2x^2 + 8x + 3 {/eq} We'll start by finding the critical point: {eq}f'(x) = 4x + 8 {/eq} {eq}0 = 4x + 8 {/eq} {eq}x = -2 {/eq} Now we'll check to see whether this function has a minimum or maximum by finding the second derivative: {eq}f''(x) = 4 {/eq} {eq}f''(-2) = 4 {/eq} With a positive value for the second derivative, this parabola should open up and therefore have a minimum value. Let's plug the critical point back into the original function to find the minimum value: {eq}f(-2) = 2 (-2)^2 + 8 (-2) + 3 {/eq} {eq}f(-2) = -5 {/eq} Therefore, our minimum value is -5 and is at the x-value of -2. So the coordinates for our vertex will be (-2,-5). The graph of this parabola will look like this: Minimum value at (-2,-5) Quadratic Maximum and Minimum Let's go through a few alternate methods to find critical points and maximum or minimum values. If we are given a quadratic in general form, we can use an equation to simulate taking the derivative: {eq}Critical Point = -b / 2a {/eq} Let's try using this example: {eq}f(x) = 3x^2 + 2x - 1 {/eq} {eq}Critical Point = -(2) / 2(3) {/eq} {eq}Critical Point = -1/3 {/eq} We can look at the a value in the general form to figure out if the parabola will open up or down, which will give us information on whether the critical point is a maximum or minimum. Since the a value of this example is positive, the parabola will open up so we have a minimum value. We can plug in this critical point to find the minimum value: {eq}f(-1/3) = 3(-1/3)^2 + 2(-1/3) -1 {/eq} {eq}f(-1/3) = -4/3 {/eq} The graph for this function looks like this: Minimum value at (-1/3,-4/3) Look at the following quadratic in standard form: {eq}f(x) = -2(x + 6)^2 +3 {/eq} When given a quadratic in standard form (or after converting to it), we can easily determine the critical point and whether the parabola will open up or down.

content.title: How to Find Extrema of Multivariable Functions
content.content: How to Find Extrema of Multivariable Functions GeeksforGeeks｡How to Find Extrema of Multivariable Functions Finding the extrema of multivariable functions is a crucial aspect of multivariable calculus. These extrema can be either maximum or minimum values, and they provide essential insights into the behavior of functions involving several variables. To determine these extrema, we first identify critical points of the function. This involves calculating the first partial derivatives of the function with respect to each variable and setting them equal to zero. This step helps us locate points where the function's rate of change is zero, indicating potential extrema. In this article, we will discuss Extrema for Multivariable Functions including methods to calculate it. Table of Content What is a Multivariable Function? Extrema in Multivariable Functions Methods to Find Extrema of Multivariable Functions Using Partial Derivatives Lagrange Multipliers Method Difference Between Extrema in Single and Multivariable Functions Conclusion Practice Problems FAQs What is a Multivariable Function? Multivariable function is a type of mathematical function that takes two or more variables as input and produces an output. These functions are used extensively in fields such as calculus, physics, engineering, and economics to model situations where the outcome depends on several factors. A multivariable function can be represented as f(x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n), where x1, x2, . . . ,xn are the input variables. For example, a function f(x, y) might represent the temperature at a point on a surface, with x and y being the coordinates of the point. Extrema in Multivariable Functions In multivariable calculus, finding the extrema (maxima and minima) of a function involves determining the points at which the function reaches its highest or lowest values within a certain region. Local Maximum: A function f(x1, x2, . . . ,xn) has a local maximum at a point a = (a1, a2, . . ., an) if there exists a neighbourhood around a such that f(a) ≥ f(x) for all points x in that neighbourhood. Local Minimum: Similarly, f(x1, x2, . . . ,xn) has a local minimum at an if there exists a neighbourhood around a such that f(a) ≤ f(x) for all points x in that neighbourhood. Global Maximum/Minimum: These are the highest and lowest values of the function over its entire domain. Methods to Find Extrema of Multivariable Functions Finding extrema (maxima and minima) of multivariable functions involves several methods, each suited to different types of functions and conditions. Some of these methods are: Using Partial Derivatives To find the extrema of multivariable function, we can use Hessian matrix and it's determinant. Hessian Matrix: H = \begin{bmatrix} f_{xx} & f_{xy} \\ f_{yx} & f_{yy} \end{bmatrix} D = det(H)=fxxfyy − (fxy)2 All the conditions for extrema are: If det(H) > 0 and fxx > 0, the function has a local minimum at the critical point. If det(H) > 0 and fxx 0 \quad \text{and} \quad f_{xx} = 2 > 0 Since D > 0 and fxx > 0, the function has a local minimum at the critical point (2, 3). Conclusion: The function f(x, y) = x^2 + y^2 - 4x - 6y + 9 has a local minimum at (2, 3). Example 2: Find the extrema of the function f(x, y) = x^3 - 3xy^2**.** Solution: Step 1: Compute the first partial derivatives and find the critical points. f_x = \frac{\partial f}{\partial x} = 3x^2 - 3y^2 f_y = \frac{\partial f}{\partial y} = -6xy Set fx = 0 and fy = 0: 3x^2 - 3y^2 = 0 \implies x^2 = y^2 \implies x = \pm y -6xy = 0 \implies x = 0 \text{ or } y = 0 Combining these, we get the critical points (0, 0), (a, a), and (a, -a). Step 2: Compute the second partial derivatives to form the Hessian matrix.

content.content: Maximum and Minimum Values Oregon State University Science｡The problem to find the minimum or maximum value of a function is encountered very frequently in geometry, mechanics, physics, and other fields. It was one of the principal incentives for the development of the calculus in the seventeenth century. Our object for this page is to give a means of locating the extrema of two variable functions. Recall the same problem in the case of single veriable function. We locate all critical points by solving f'(x) = 0. It is the same as to find all points with horizontal tangent line since at the points where a differentiable function attains relative maximum or minimum the tangent line is horizontal. Similarly, for the case of a two variable differentiable function f(x, y), we look for those points (also called critical or stationary points) whose tangent planes are horizontal. Since the normal vector of tangent plane at (a, b) for the surface z = f(x, y) is we want to solve and for critical points because horizontal planes have normal vector parallel to z-axis, i.e. (0, 0, 1) or (0, 0, -1). Example 1 Find all critical points of the surface . Solution First of all, we compute Set both partial derivatives zero, we have x = 1, or -1 and y = 0. Therefore (1, 0) and (-1, 0) are the critical points of f. In the single variable problem, we have the rules to categorize the nature of critical points. There is an analogous theory, second-derivative test for extrema, for functions of two variables: Theorem Suppose (a, b) is a stationary point of a function f(x, y) with continuous second order partial derivatives in a domain containing (a, b). Let and let Then we have: With this theorem we can summarize the procedure to find the extrema of a twice diffenentiable function f(x, y) of two variables as follows: Step 1 Locate the critical points by solving and . Step 2 Compute second partial derivatives and and evaluate the for each critical point found in step 1. Step 3 Use the Theorem above to categorize the nature of critical points. Then compare their function values to find the absolute maximum or minimum. Step 4 If the function is restricted to a domain (finite) with boundary, we should also search for the extrema along the boundary. It is then reduced to a single variable problem theoretically. Example 2 Find all relative maximums and minimums for the function Solution Step 1. Compute the first order partial derivatives and set to zero. we have x = 0 or 2 and y = 1 or -1. Thus (0, 1), (0, -1), (2, 1) and (2, -1) are the critical points of f. Step 2 After some computations, we have Note that f is an exponential function, always positive. Step 3 From the Theorem, we know that f(0, 1) = exp(2/3) is a relative maximum and f(2,-1) = exp(-14/3) is a relative minimum. At both (0, -1) and (2, 1), f has saddle points. Along y = 0, x-axis, it is easy to see that It shows that f can grow as big as possible when x tends to infinity and as close to zero as well when x tends negative infinity (note f is positive for all (x, y)), so we conclude that f has no absolute maximum nor absolute minimum over xy-plane. Suppose the problem was further restricted to the region R bounded by y = -x + 4 and , then we have more (step 4) to search for the possible extrema along boundaries. In this case, only (2, 1) and (2, -1) are inside R, they are still saddle point and relative minimum respectively. Step 4 The restriction of f on the boundary of R can be expressed as respectively. Both are reduced to single variable problems. Readers should be able to find the maximums and minimums on each restriction. To determine the absolute extrema on the region R, you need to compare the function values of all critical points obtained in step 3 and 4 and corner points, such as the intersection points of two boundary curves.

Let n be 22...22, with a total of 1980 digits. What is n mod 1982?

My current view is that the answer is 2.
My reason is: In the repunit formula n=2(10^1980-1)/9, I replace the power 10^1980 by 10 under the modulus. This leaves 2(10-1)/9=2.

content.text:
Looking at this problem, I need to compute n mod 1982 where n = 222...2 (1980 twos).

**Setting up the formula:**
$$n = 2 \cdot \underbrace{111\ldots1}_{1980 \text{ ones}} = 2 \cdot R_{1980}$$

where $R_{1980} = \frac{10^{1980} - 1}{9}$.

**Your proposed approach (reducing 10^1980 → 10):**
$$n \equiv 2 \cdot \frac{10 - 1}{9} = 2 \pmod{1982}$$

This only works if $R_{1980} \equiv 1 \pmod{1982}$, i.e., if $10^{1980} \equiv 10 \pmod{9 \cdot 1982}$.

By Fermat/Euler, $10^{\gcd(1980, 9\cdot 1981)} = 10^{\gcd(1980, 17829)}$ must be checked. Since $\gcd(1980, 17829) = 1$ (because $17829 = 9 \cdot 1981$ and $1981$ is prime, neither divides 1980), we actually get $10^{1980} \equiv 1 \pmod{1981}$ (Fermat). So $10^{1980} \equiv 1 \pmod{9 \cdot 1982 = 17838}$ does **not** hold in general.

**Correct approach: use CRT with 1982 = 2 × 991.**

**Mod 2:** $n = \underbrace{222\ldots2}_{1980} \equiv 0 \pmod 2$ (since $2 \equiv 0$).

**Mod 991:** By Fermat's little theorem, $10^{990} \equiv 1 \pmod{991}$.
Note $1980 = 2 \cdot 990$, so $10^{1980} \equiv 1 \pmod{991}$.

$$R_{1980} = \frac{10^{1980} - 1}{9}$$

Since $10 \equiv 1 \pmod 9$, $10^{1980} \equiv 1 \pmod 9$, so $10^{1980} - 1 = 9k$ for some integer. Also $10^{1980} \equiv 1 \pmod{991}$, so $9k \equiv 0 \pmod{991}$. Since $\gcd(9, 991) = 1$:
$$R_{1980} \equiv \frac{10^{1980} - 1}{9} \equiv \frac{1 - 1}{9} \equiv 0 \pmod{991}$$

So $n \equiv 2 \cdot 0 = 0 \pmod{991}$, and $n \equiv 0 \pmod 2$.

**By CRT:** $n \equiv 0 \pmod{1982}$.

Let me verify with a small case. Take $n = 22$ (two 2's), so $n \bmod 1982 = 22$. The formula $R_2 = 11$, $n = 22$, and indeed $22 \equiv 0 \pmod 2$, $22 \equiv 22 \pmod{991}$. This is a 2-digit example so different.

For 1980 digits, the structure gives $n \equiv 0 \pmod{1982}$.

The core update formulas are an+1=an+bn2, a_{n+1} = \frac{a_n + b_n}{2}, an+1=2an+bn, bn+1=anbn. b_{n+1} = \sqrt{a_n b_n}. bn+1=anbn. These steps are repeated for successive nnn, with the difference an−bna_n - b_nan−bn decreasing monotonically to zero.7 Each iteration approximately doubles the precision of the sequences due to quadratic convergence, allowing rapid achievement of high accuracy with relatively few steps. The updates are performed in the order shown to minimize rounding errors in floating-point implementations.19 Termination and Output The Gauss–Legendre algorithm employs a stopping criterion based on the convergence of the iterates, typically continuing the iteration until the absolute difference between the current arithmetic mean ana_nan and geometric mean bnb_nbn satisfies ∣an−bn∣ 0 $ depending on the initial conditions, implying $ \log_{10} d_n \approx n \log_{10} 2 + \const $. This rapid growth underscores the algorithm's superiority over linearly convergent methods for high-precision tasks.23 However, practical implementation faces limitations with standard floating-point arithmetic, which typically provides only about 15 decimal digits of precision in double-precision format. content.title: Arithmetic–geometric mean
content.content: Arithmetic–geometric mean Wikiwand｡Arithmetic–geometric mean Mathematical function of two positive real arguments From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia This article is about the particular type of mean. For the similarly named inequality, see Inequality of arithmetic and geometric means. In mathematics, the arithmetic–geometric mean (AGM or agM) of two positive real numbers x and y is the mutual limit of a sequence of arithmetic means and a sequence of geometric means. The arithmetic–geometric mean is used in fast algorithms for exponential, trigonometric functions, and other special functions, as well as some mathematical constants, in particular, computing π. Plot of the arithmetic–geometric mean agm ⁡ ( 1 , x ) {\displaystyle \operatorname {agm} (1,x)} among several generalized means. The AGM is defined as the limit of the interdependent sequences a i {\displaystyle a_{i}} and g i {\displaystyle g_{i}} . Assuming x ≥ y ≥ 0 {\displaystyle x\geq y\geq 0} , we write: a 0 = x , g 0 = y a n + 1 = 1 2 ( a n + g n ) , g n + 1 = a n g n . {\displaystyle {\begin{aligned}a_{0}&=x,\\g_{0}&=y\\a_{n+1}&={\tfrac {1}{2}}(a_{n}+g_{n}),\\g_{n+1}&={\sqrt {a_{n}g_{n}}}\,.\end{aligned}}} These two sequences converge to the same number, the arithmetic–geometric mean of x and y; it is denoted by M(x, y), or sometimes by agm(x, y) or AGM(x, y). The arithmetic–geometric mean can be extended to complex numbers and, when the branches of the square root are allowed to be taken inconsistently, it is a multivalued function. Example To find the arithmetic–geometric mean of a0 = 24 and g0 = 6, iterate as follows: a 1 = 1 2 ( 24 + 6 ) = 15 g 1 = 24 ⋅ 6 = 12 a 2 = 1 2 ( 15 + 12 ) = 13.5 g 2 = 15 ⋅ 12 = 13.416 407 8649 … ⋮ {\displaystyle {\begin{array}{rcccl}a_{1}&=&{\tfrac {1}{2}}(24+6)&=&15\\g_{1}&=&{\sqrt {24\cdot 6}}&=&12\\a_{2}&=&{\tfrac {1}{2}}(15+12)&=&13.5\\g_{2}&=&{\sqrt {15\cdot 12}}&=&13.416\ 407\ 8649\dots \\&&\vdots &&\end{array}}} The first five iterations give the following values: More information n, an ... The number of digits in which a**n and g**n agree (underlined) approximately doubles with each iteration. The arithmetic–geometric mean of 24 and 6 is the common limit of these two sequences, which is approximately 13.4581714817256154207668131569743992430538388544. History The first algorithm based on this sequence pair appeared in the works of Lagrange. Its properties were further analyzed by Gauss. Properties Both the geometric mean and arithmetic mean of two positive numbers x and y are between the two numbers. (They are strictly between when x ≠ y.) The geometric mean of two positive numbers is never greater than the arithmetic mean. So the geometric means are an increasing sequence g0 ≤ g1 ≤ g2 ≤ ...; the arithmetic means are a decreasing sequence a0 ≥ a1 ≥ a2 ≥ ...; and gn ≤ M(x, y) ≤ an for any n. These are strict inequalities if x ≠ y. M(x, y) is thus a number between x and y; it is also between the geometric and arithmetic mean of x and y. If r ≥ 0 then M(rx, ry) = r M(x, y).

content.title: Arithmetic-Geometric Mean — Definition, Formula & Examples
content.content: Arithmetic-Geometric Mean — Definition, Formula & Examples Mathwords｡Arithmetic-Geometric Mean — Definition, Formula & Examples The arithmetic-geometric mean (AGM) of two positive numbers is the common limit reached by repeatedly taking their arithmetic mean and geometric mean in tandem. Both sequences converge rapidly to a single value that lies between the original geometric and arithmetic means. Given two positive real numbers a0a_0a0 and b0b_0b0, define the sequences an+1=an+bn2a_{n+1} = \frac{a_n + b_n}{2}an+1=2an+bn and bn+1=an bnb_{n+1} = \sqrt{a_n , b_n}bn+1=anbn. These sequences converge to a common limit M(a0,b0)M(a_0, b_0)M(a0,b0), called the arithmetic-geometric mean, satisfying min⁡(a0,b0)≤M(a0,b0)≤max⁡(a0,b0)\min(a_0, b_0) \le M(a_0, b_0) \le \max(a_0, b_0)min(a0,b0)≤M(a0,b0)≤max(a0,b0). Key Formula an+1=an+bn2,bn+1=an bna_{n+1} = \frac{a_n + b_n}{2}, \qquad b_{n+1} = \sqrt{a_n , b_n}an+1=2an+bn,bn+1=anbn Where: ana_nan = The arithmetic-mean sequence value at step n bnb_nbn = The geometric-mean sequence value at step n M(a0,b0)M(a_0, b_0)M(a0,b0) = The common limit of both sequences (the AGM) How It Works Start with two positive numbers a0a_0a0 and b0b_0b0. At each step, replace them with their arithmetic mean and geometric mean. The arithmetic mean is always at least as large as the geometric mean (by the AM-GM inequality), so the two sequences squeeze together. Convergence is quadratic, meaning the number of correct digits roughly doubles with each iteration. After just a few steps, the two values agree to many decimal places. content.content: Arithmetic–geometric mean HandWiki｡Arithmetic–geometric mean More More Languages Page actions Read History Revision as of 22:16, 11 February 2026 by Len Stevenson (talk | contribs) (update) (diff) ← Older revision | Latest revision (diff) | Newer revision → (diff) Short description: Mathematical function of two positive real arguments This article is about the particular type of mean. For the similarly named inequality, see Inequality of arithmetic and geometric means. Plot of the arithmetic–geometric mean agm⁡(1,x) among several generalized means. In mathematics, the arithmetic–geometric mean (AGM or agM) of two positive real numbers x and y is the mutual limit of a sequence of arithmetic means and a sequence of geometric means. The arithmetic–geometric mean is used in fast algorithms for exponential, trigonometric functions, and other special functions, as well as some mathematical constants, in particular, computing π. The AGM is defined as the limit of the interdependent sequences ai and gi. Assuming x≥y≥0, we write:a0=x,g0=yan+1=12(an+gn),gn+1=angn.These two sequences converge to the same number, the arithmetic–geometric mean of x and y; it is denoted by M(x, y), or sometimes by agm(x, y) or AGM(x, y). The arithmetic–geometric mean can be extended to complex numbers and, when the branches of the square root are allowed to be taken inconsistently, it is a multivalued function. Contents 1 Example 2 History 3 Properties 4 Related concepts 5 Proof of existence 6 Proof of the integral-form expression 7 Applications 7.1 The number π 7.2 Complete elliptic integral K(sinα) 7.3 Other applications 8 See also 9 References 9.1 Notes 9.2 Citations 9.3 Sources Example To find the arithmetic–geometric mean of a0 = 24 and g0 = 6, iterate as follows:a1=12(24+6)=15g1=24⋅6=12a2=12(15+12)=13.5g2=15⋅12=13.416 407 8649…⋮The first five iterations give the following values: n a n g n 0 24 6 1 1 5 1 2 2 13 .5 13 .416 407 864 998 738 178 455 042... 3 13.458 203 932 499 369 089 227 521... 13.458 139 030 990 984 877 207 090... 4 13.458 171 481 7 45 176 983 217 305... 13.458 171 481 7 06 053 858 316 334... 5 13.458 171 481 725 615 420 766 8 20... 13.458 171 481 725 615 420 766 8 06... The number of digits in which an and gn agree (underlined) approximately doubles with each iteration. The arithmetic–geometric mean of 24 and 6 is the common limit of these two sequences, which is approximately 13.4581714817256154207668131569743992430538388544. History The first algorithm based on this sequence pair appeared in the works of Lagrange. Its properties were further analyzed by Gauss. Properties Both the geometric mean and arithmetic mean of two positive numbers x and y are between the two numbers. (They are strictly between when x ≠ y.) The geometric mean of two positive numbers is never greater than the arithmetic mean. So the geometric means are an increasing sequence g0 ≤ g1 ≤ g2 ≤ ...; the arithmetic means are a decreasing sequence a0 ≥ a1 ≥ a2 ≥ ...;

content.title: Sophie Germain's Identity
content.content: Sophie Germain's Identity Cut-the-Knot｡An identity named after the famous french mathematician Sophie Germain (1776 - 1831) is a useful tool for math olympians: a4+4b4=(a2+2b2−2ab)(a2+2b2+2ab). The proof is by direct verification. Here's a problem that is easily solved with Sophie Germain's identity: Is 20154+42015 prime? Due to Sophie Germain's identity the answer is negative. Indeed, 20154+42015=20154+4⋅42014=20154+4⋅24028=20154+4⋅(21007)4=(20152+22015−2015⋅21008)(20152+22015+2015⋅21008). Since the second factor is clearly greater than 1, we only need to check that this is also true for the first factor. But 21007>211=2048>2015, implying that 22015>2015⋅21008. In fact, n4+4n, where n is a positive integer, is never a prime for n>1. It is even if n is even, and, if n is odd, we can simply generalize the above derivation. References A. Engel, Problem-Solving Strategies, Springer Verlag, 1998, p 121

content.content: CHAMP Dataset Explorer｡ Besides the concept above, you may also find the following information useful: 1. Separately consider the cases of even and odd n>1. To solve this problem, we will consider the cases where \( n \) is even and where \( n \) is odd separately. **Case 1: \( n \) is even** If \( n \) is even, then \( n = 2k \) for some integer \( k \). The expression \( n^4 + 4^n \) can be rewritten using the fact that \( 4^n = (2^2)^n = 2^{2n} \) and applying Sophie Germain's identity with \( a = n^2 \) and \( b = 2^n \): \[ n^4 + 4^n = (2k)^4 + 4^{2k} = (2^2k^2)^2 + 2^{4k} = (2^{2k^2})^2 + (2^{2k})^2 \] Now, we can apply Sophie Germain's identity: \[ n^4 + 4^n = (n^2 + 2 \cdot 2^n)^2 - (2 \cdot n \cdot 2^n)^2 \] \[ n^4 + 4^n = (n^2 + 2^{n+1})^2 - (2n \cdot 2^n)^2 \] \[ n^4 + 4^n = (n^2 + 2^{n+1} + 2n \cdot 2^n)(n^2 + 2^{n+1} - 2n \cdot 2^n) \] Since \( n \) is even, both \( n^2 + 2^{n+1} + 2n \cdot 2^n \) and \( n^2 + 2^{n+1} - 2n \cdot 2^n \) are greater than 1, which means that \( n^4 + 4^n \) is not prime for even \( n > 1 \). **Case 2: \( n \) is odd** If \( n \) is odd, then \( n^4 + 4^n \) is the sum of an odd number and an even number, which is always odd. Therefore, it could potentially be prime. However, we need to check if it is actually prime for any odd \( n \) in the given set. For \( n = 1 \), we have: \[ n^4 + 4^n = 1^4 + 4^1 = 1 + 4 = 5 \] The number 5 is prime, so \( n = 1 \) is one solution. For odd \( n > 1 \), we can factor \( 4^n \) as \( (2^2)^n = 2^{2n} \), and since \( n \) is odd, \( 2n \) is even, and we can write \( 2^{2n} \) as \( (2^n)^2 \). Now, we can use a similar approach to the even case by adding and subtracting \( 4n^2 \) to create a sum of two squares: \[ n^4 + 4^n = n^4 + 4 \cdot (2^n)^2 = n^4 + 4n^2 + 4 \cdot (2^n)^2 - 4n^2 \] \[ n^4 + 4^n = (n^2 + 2 \cdot 2^n)^2 - (2n)^2 \] Now, we can apply the difference of squares formula: \[ n^4 + 4^n = [(n^2 + 2 \cdot 2^n) + 2n] \cdot [(n^2 + 2 \cdot 2^n) - 2n] \] Since \( n \) is odd and greater than 1, both \( (n^2 + 2 \cdot 2^n) + 2n \) and \( (n^2 + 2 \cdot 2^n) - 2n \) are greater than 1, which means that \( n^4 + 4^n \) is not prime for odd \( n > 1 \). **Conclusion** The only integer \( n \) in the set {1, 2, ..., 99} for which \( n^4 + 4^n \) is prime is \( n = 1 \). For all other values of \( n \), the expression \( n^4 + 4^n \) is not prime. Therefore, there is only 1 integer \( n \) in the given set for which \( n^4 + 4^n \) is prime. Now, summarize the answer above in one sentence, without any intermediate steps or explanations. There is only one integer \( n \) in the set {1, 2, ..., 99} for which \( n^4 + 4^n \) is prime, and that is \( n = 1 \).

content.title: Sophie Germain's identity
content.content: Sophie Germain's identity The On-Line Encyclopedia of Integer Sequences｡Sophie Germain's identity pertains to sums of fourth powers. Theorem. (Sophie Germain) Given real numbers x and y, x4+4y4=(x2−2xy+2y2)(x2+2xy+2y2). Proof. Rewrite x4+4y4 as (x2)2+(2y2)2+2x22y2−2x22y2, which can then be rewritten as (x2+2y2)2−(2xy)2 and finally (x2−2xy+2y2)(x2+2xy+2y2) as specified by the theorem. □ It may perhaps seem unnecessary to mention that the identity holds true if x or y or both are negative. Even-indexed powers of negative numbers are positive, so the left hand side of the equation is the same if we multiply xy or both by –1. If just one of them is negative, the right hand side changes subtly but without affecting the overall result: −2xy becomes a positive number but then 2xy becomes a negative number. For this reason we may safely ignore x, y value pairs containing negative numbers. Applications for results on prime numbers Theorem 5.1 The only prime number of the form x4+4y4 is 5. Proof. Assume x4+4y4 is prime. Sophie Germain's identity exposes two divisors of a number of this form, and since a prime number has only two distinct divisors, this must mean that x2+2xy+2y2=x4+4y4 and x2−2xy+2y2=1. Satisfying the latter equation is a necessary (but not sufficient) condition for the primality of x4+4y4. That equation has only four solutions, of which we will ignore the two solutions with negative numbers as they lead to the same results as their absolute values. This leaves x=1, y=0 and x=1, y=1. The former solution leads to x4+4y4=1, which is not prime, the latter to x4+4y4=5, which is prime. Since we have now examined all the solutions to x2−2xy+2y2=1, we can now be certain we have identified the only prime of the form x4+4y4, namely 5, as specified by the theorem. □ In this next one it is a little less obvious we can use Sophie Germain's identity. Theorem 5.2 The only prime of the form n4+4n is 5. Proof. Before we can apply Sophie Germain's identity, we need to express 4n as a number of the form 4y2. Clearly 2 is not a number of the form n4+4n, which leaves odd primes, and so n must be odd or else it will certainly not produce an odd prime in the formula. This fact allows us to rewrite 4n as 42k+1=4(2k)4. Now we can simply invoke Theorem 5.1, and thus the present theorem follows naturally. □ As it turns out, it is not actually necessary to apply Sophie Germain's identity to prove 5.2, but for the sake of reference here it goes: n4+4(2k)4=(n2−n2k+1+22k+1)(n2+n2k+1+22k+1).

content.title: Safe and Sophie Germain primes - Wikipedia Republished // WIKI 2
content.content: Safe and Sophie Germain primes - Wikipedia Republished // WIKI 2 Wiki2｡Safe and Sophie Germain primes From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia A prime pair (p, 2p+1) In number theory, a prime number p is a Sophie Germain prime if 2p + 1 is also prime. The number 2p + 1 associated with a Sophie Germain prime is called a safe prime. For example, 11 is a Sophie Germain prime and 2 × 11 + 1 = 23 is its associated safe prime. Sophie Germain primes and safe primes have applications in public key cryptography and primality testing. It has been conjectured that there are infinitely many Sophie Germain primes, but this remains unproven. Sophie Germain primes are named after French mathematician Sophie Germain, who used them in her investigations of Fermat's Last Theorem. One attempt by Germain to prove Fermat’s Last Theorem was to let p be a prime number of the form 8k + 7 and to let n = p – 1. In this case, x n + y n = z n {\displaystyle x^{n}+y^{n}=z^{n}} is unsolvable. Germain’s proof, however, remained unfinished. Through her attempts to solve Fermat's Last Theorem, Germain developed a result now known as Germain's Theorem which states that if p is an odd prime and 2p + 1 is also prime, then p must divide x, y, or z. Otherwise, x n + y n ≠ z n {\textstyle x^{n}+y^{n}\neq z^{n}} . This case where p does not divide x, y, or z is called the first case. Sophie Germain’s work was the most progress achieved on Fermat’s last theorem at that time. Later work by Kummer and others always divided the problem into first and second cases. content.title: Sophie Germain's identity
content.content: Sophie Germain's identity Kiwix维基百科镜像｡In mathematics, Sophie Germain's identity is a polynomial factorization named after Sophie Germain stating that x 4 + 4 y 4 = ( ( x + y ) 2 + y 2 ) ⋅ ( ( x − y ) 2 + y 2 ) = ( x 2 + 2 x y + 2 y 2 ) ⋅ ( x 2 − 2 x y + 2 y 2 ) . {\displaystyle {\begin{aligned}x^{4}+4y^{4}&={\bigl (}(x+y)^{2}+y^{2}{\bigr )}\cdot {\bigl (}(x-y)^{2}+y^{2}{\bigr )}\\&=(x^{2}+2xy+2y^{2})\cdot (x^{2}-2xy+2y^{2}).\end{aligned}}} Beyond its use in elementary algebra, it can also be used in number theory to factorize integers of the special form x 4 + 4 y 4 {\displaystyle x^{4}+4y^{4}} , and it frequently forms the basis of problems in mathematics competitions. History Although the identity has been attributed to Sophie Germain, it does not appear in her works. Instead, in her works one can find the related identity x 4 + y 4 = ( x 2 − y 2 ) 2 + 2 ( x y ) 2 = ( x 2 + y 2 ) 2 − 2 ( x y ) 2 . {\displaystyle {\begin{aligned}x^{4}+y^{4}&=(x^{2}-y^{2})^{2}+2(xy)^{2}\\&=(x^{2}+y^{2})^{2}-2(xy)^{2}.\\\end{aligned}}} Modifying this equation by multiplying y {\displaystyle y} by 2 {\displaystyle {\sqrt {2}}} gives x 4 + 4 y 4 = ( x 2 + 2 y 2 ) 2 − 4 ( x y ) 2 , {\displaystyle x^{4}+4y^{4}=(x^{2}+2y^{2})^{2}-4(xy)^{2},} a difference of two squares, from which Germain's identity follows. The inaccurate attribution of this identity to Germain was made by Leonard Eugene Dickson in his History of the Theory of Numbers, which also stated (equally inaccurately) that it could be found in a letter from Leonhard Euler to Christian Goldbach. The identity can be proven simply by multiplying the two terms of the factorization together, and verifying that their product equals the right hand side of the equality. A proof without words is also possible based on multiple applications of the Pythagorean theorem. Applications to integer factorization One consequence of Germain's identity is that the numbers of the form n 4 + 4 n {\displaystyle n^{4}+4^{n}} cannot be prime for n > 1 {\displaystyle n>1} . (For n = 1 {\displaystyle n=1} , the result is the prime number 5.) They are obviously not prime if n {\displaystyle n} is even, and if n {\displaystyle n} is odd they have a factorization given by the identity with x = n {\displaystyle x=n} and y = 2 ( n − 1 ) / 2 {\displaystyle y=2^{(n-1)/2}} . These numbers (starting with n = 0 {\displaystyle n=0} ) form the integer sequence 1, 5, 32, 145, 512, 1649, 5392, 18785, 69632, ... (sequence A001589 in the OEIS). Many of the appearances of Sophie Germain's identity in mathematics competitions come from this corollary of it.

content.title: A simpler argument to prove n4  4n is composite for n ending in 5?
content.content: A simpler argument to prove n^4 + 4^n is composite for n ending in 5? Mathematics Stack Exchange｡A simpler argument to prove n^4 + 4^n is composite for n ending in 5? The expression $n^4 + \,4^n$ is known to be prime only for $n = 1$ corresponding to the prime $5$. The usual proof makes use of the Sophie Germain identity $$a^4 + \,4b^4 ≡ \left\{(a - b)^2 +\, b^2\right\}\left\{(a + b)^2 +\, b^2\right\}$$ since $n^4 + \,4^n$ is odd only for odd $n$ in which case $4^n$ has the form $4\left(2^k\right)^4$ and then both factors $\left(n ± 2^k\right)^2 + \,4^k > 1$ for $ k > 0 $. We observe, on the other hand, that for all $n$ ending in $1, 3, 7, 9$ expression ends in $5$ and obviously cannot be prime. I was wondering if a similar line of thought could dispose of the case when $n$ ends in $5$, but here I can't proceed further beyond the fact that they generate numbers ending in $49$ and primes do end in $49$ and hence doesn't preclude the existence of a prime. Can we somehow obviate recourse to Sophie Germain identity (or the like) to prove the expression is composite also in the case $n$ ending in $5$ ? In general for non negative $a,b$ $$a^2+b^2 = (a -\sqrt{2ab}+b)(a +\sqrt{2ab}+b)$$ so you can say $$n^4 + 4^n = (n^2 - 2^{\frac{(n+1)}2}n +2^n)(n^2 + 2^{\frac{(n+1)}2}n +2^n)$$ which is the product of two integers when $n$ is odd, and both those integers are greater than $1$ when $n\ge 3$. Numbers ending in $5$ are odd and greater than $3$. HenryHenry 160k99 gold badges128128 silver badges267267 bronze badges

1324 persons are arranged in a circle and numbered from 1 to 1324. Then every 2nd person is removed (i.e., the first four removed people are those numbered 2, 4, 6 and 8) until there is only one person left. What is the number of the last person left?

content.text:
Looking at this problem, I need to find the last person remaining when every 2nd person is removed in a circular arrangement, starting with person 2.

This is the classic Josephus problem with k=2, starting from position 1.

**My analysis:**

For the standard Josephus problem with n people and every 2nd person eliminated, when n is a power of 2, the survivor is person n.

For general n, the formula can be derived by considering what happens after one complete round of eliminations.

After the first pass, all even-numbered people are removed. The remaining people are the odd numbers: 1, 3, 5, ..., 1323.

If we relabel these odd positions as 1, 2, 3, ..., 662 (by mapping position 2k-1 to new position k), then we have a similar problem with 662 people, but the next elimination begins with person 2 in the new labeling (since person 4 in original was eliminated last in the first round, making person 3 the next to start).

Wait, let me reconsider. After removing 2, 4, 6, 8, the next person to remove is... person 1 remains, then we continue removing every 2nd, so person 10 is next. The remaining set after first pass is {1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11, ...}, and the elimination continues with person 10 removed (equivalent to position 5 in odd-numbered list), then 14, etc.

messages.content: Let n be 22...22, with a total of 1980 digits. What is n mod 1982?

content.text:
The number is \(n=22\cdots 22\) with 1980 digits, so

\[
n = 2\cdot\frac{10^{1980}-1}{9}.
\]

We need \(n \bmod 1982\). Note \(1982 = 2\cdot 991\), with \(991\) prime.

Modulo \(991\): by Fermat, \(10^{990}\equiv 1 \pmod{991}\). Since \(1980=2\cdot 990\),

\[
10^{1980}\equiv 1 \pmod{991}.
\]

Thus

\[
9n = 2(10^{1980}-1)\equiv 0 \pmod{991}.
\]

Since \(\gcd(9,991)=1\), we get \(991\mid n\). Also \(n\) is even, so \(2\mid n\). Therefore \(1982=2\cdot 991\mid n\).

Hence

\[
n \bmod 1982 = 0.
\]

Solve the following problem. Make sure to show your work before giving the final answer. Find the minimum value of a^4+b^4+c^4-a^2*bc-b^2*ac-c^2*ab for positive numbers a, b, c. This problem can be solved using the AM-GM inequality (Arithmetic Mean-Geometric Mean Inequality). The AM-GM inequality states that the arithmetic mean of non-negative real numbers is greater than or equal to the geometric mean. In other words, if x1, x2, ..., xn are non-negative real numbers, then: (x1 + x2 + ... + xn) / n ≥ √[x1 * x2 * ... * xn] Let's apply this inequality to the given problem. We can rewrite the expression as follows: a^4 + b^4 + c^4 - a^2*bc - b^2*ac - c^2*ab = (a^4 - a^2*bc) + (b^4 - b^2*ac) + (c^4 - c^2*ab) = a^2*(a^2 - bc) + b^2*(b^2 - ac) + c^2*(c^2 - ab) Now, we apply the AM-GM inequality to each of the three terms: a^2*(a^2 - bc) ≥ 2*a*√[a^2*(a^2 - bc)] b^2*(b^2 - ac) ≥ 2*b*√[b^2*(b^2 - ac)] c^2*(c^2 - ab) ≥ 2*c*√[c^2*(c^2 - ab)] Adding these inequalities, we get: a^2*(a^2 - bc) + b^2*(b^2 - ac) + c^2*(c^2 - ab) ≥ 2*(a*√[a^2*(a^2 - bc)] + b*√[b^2*(b^2 - ac)] + c*√[c^2*(c^2 - ab)]) Now, we apply the AM-GM inequality again to the right side of the inequality: 2*(a*√[a^2*(a^2 - bc)] + b*√[b^2*(b^2 - ac)] + c*√[c^2*(c^2 - ab)]) ≥ 2*√[3*(a*b*c)^2] So, we have: a^2*(a^2 - bc) + b^2*(b^2 - ac) + c^2*(c^2 - ab) ≥ 2*√[3*(a*b*c)^2] Therefore, the minimum value of a^4 + b^4 + c^4 - a^2*bc - b^2*ac - c^2*ab for positive numbers a, b, c is 2*√[3*(a*b*c)^2]. Now, summarize the answer above in one sentence, without any intermediate steps or explanations. The minimum value of the expression a^4 + b^4 + c^4 - a^2*bc - b^2*ac - c^2*ab for positive numbers a, b, c is 2*√[3*(a*b*c)^2].

Show that $a^4+b^4+c^4 \geq a+b+c$ My idea We can write the inequality as $4a^4+4b^4+4c^4\geq 4a^2bc+ 4b^2ac+ 4c^2ab$ which is true by AM-GM ($2a^4+b^4+c^4 \geq 4a^2bc$) Is my idea right? I am in doubt because the numbers have to be real, and it doesn't specify if they are negative or positive. Because the question allows for all reals, your solution is likely worth $0^+$. It could depend on the strictness of the grader, but I believe that the phrasing is meant to catch those who blindly use AM-GM without accounting for the non-negative conditions. Your solution can be fixed by saying that $$ 2a^4 + b^4 + c^4 \geq 4|a^2bc| = 4|a| \geq 4a.$$ We satisfied the non-negative condition in AM-GM using the terms $a^2, b^2, c^2$. answered Dec 19, 2024 at 22:05 We need to show for all non-zero $a, b, c \in \mathbb R$, the inequality: $$a^4 + b^4 + c^4 ≥ a + b + c$$ holds true given that $abc = 1$. CASE 1: $a, b, c \in \mathbb R^+$ By the AM ≥ GM inequality (for positive reals): $$\dfrac{2a^4 + b^4 + c^4}{4} ≥ \sqrt{a^4(abc)^4} = a$$ Continuing this process for $b, c$ and then adding all the inequalities up will yield: $$\therefore a^4 + b^4 + c^4 ≥ a + b + c \longleftarrow \forall\ a, b, c \in \mathbb R^+$$ Note that equality will only hold when $a^4 = b^4 = c^4$ as per the AM ≥ GM inequality. Since this case deals with positive reals, $a = b = c = 1$ will result in equality because $a^4b^4c^4 = 1$. Case 2: $a, b, c \in \mathbb R$ Now, we include negative reals too. WLOG, suppose that $a a + b + c$$ Thus, we have shown in all cases that: $$\boxed{a^4 + b^4 + c^4 ≥ a + b + c}$$ where equality holds if and only if $a = b = c = 1$. $\blacksquare$ answered Dec 17, 2024 at 11:07 Here is a solution by using sum of squares $\geq 0$. Homogenize the initial inequality to get $$a^4 + b^4 + c^4 \geq abc(a+b+c)$$ But is true for $a,b,c\in \mathbb R$ that $$(a^2-b^2)^2 + (b^2-c^2)^2 + (c^2-a^2)^2 + (ac-bc)^2 + (ab-ac)^2 + (bc-ab)^2\geq 0$$ which is equivalent to $2a^4 + 2b^4 + 2c^4 - 2a^2bc - 2b^2ac - 2c^2ab\geq 0$ which is the same as $a^4+b^4+c^4\geq abc(a+b+c)$.

We have:
- u_n = (u_{n-1} + v_{n-1})/2
- v_n = (u_{n-1} + 2v_{n-1})/3

Let d_n = u_n - v_n. Then:

= [3(u_{n-1}+v_{n-1}) - 2(u_{n-1}+2v_{n-1})]/6

= [3u_{n-1}+3v_{n-1} - 2u_{n-1}-4v_{n-1}]/6

= [u_{n-1} - v_{n-1}]/6

So d_n = d_0 / 6^n.

Since |1/6| < 1, d_n → 0. Therefore L_u - L_v = 0.

Note the sequences both converge (the transformation matrix has eigenvalues 1 and 1/6, so it's a contraction on the difference), and their limits are equal.

content.text:
Let me solve this directly.

We want to minimize
$$F = a^2+b^2+c^2-(ab+bc+ac)-(a+b+c)$$
subject to $a+b+c=9$, so $a+b+c=9$ and $F = a^2+b^2+c^2-(ab+bc+ac)-9$.

Let $s=a+b+c=9$ and $q=ab+bc+ac$. Then
$$a^2+b^2+c^2 = s^2-2q = 81-2q.$$
So
$$F = (81-2q) - q - 9 = 72 - 3q.$$

Thus minimizing $F$ is equivalent to maximizing $q=ab+bc+ac$ subject to $a+b+c=9$.

For real $a,b,c$ with fixed sum, the maximum of $q$ occurs at $a=b=c=3$, giving $q=27$.

Check: $q\le s^2/3 = 27$ since $(a-b)^2+(b-c)^2+(c-a)^2\ge 0$ implies $q\le s^2/3$.

Therefore minimum $F = 72 - 3(27) = 72 - 81 = -9$.

Attained at $a=b=c=3$.

Final answer: $-9$.```json

Solve the following problem. Make sure to show your work before giving the final answer. Find the minimum value of a^4+b^4+c^4-a^2*bc-b^2*ac-c^2*ab for positive numbers a, b, c. This problem can be solved using the AM-GM inequality (Arithmetic Mean-Geometric Mean Inequality). The AM-GM inequality states that the arithmetic mean of non-negative real numbers is greater than or equal to the geometric mean. In other words, if x1, x2, ..., xn are non-negative real numbers, then: (x1 + x2 + ... + xn) / n ≥ √[x1 * x2 * ... * xn] Let's apply this inequality to the given problem. We can rewrite the expression as follows: a^4 + b^4 + c^4 - a^2*bc - b^2*ac - c^2*ab = (a^4 - a^2*bc) + (b^4 - b^2*ac) + (c^4 - c^2*ab) = a^2*(a^2 - bc) + b^2*(b^2 - ac) + c^2*(c^2 - ab) Now, we apply the AM-GM inequality to each of the three terms: a^2*(a^2 - bc) ≥ 2*a*√[a^2*(a^2 - bc)] b^2*(b^2 - ac) ≥ 2*b*√[b^2*(b^2 - ac)] c^2*(c^2 - ab) ≥ 2*c*√[c^2*(c^2 - ab)] Adding these inequalities, we get: a^2*(a^2 - bc) + b^2*(b^2 - ac) + c^2*(c^2 - ab) ≥ 2*(a*√[a^2*(a^2 - bc)] + b*√[b^2*(b^2 - ac)] + c*√[c^2*(c^2 - ab)]) Now, we apply the AM-GM inequality again to the right side of the inequality: 2*(a*√[a^2*(a^2 - bc)] + b*√[b^2*(b^2 - ac)] + c*√[c^2*(c^2 - ab)]) ≥ 2*√[3*(a*b*c)^2] So, we have: a^2*(a^2 - bc) + b^2*(b^2 - ac) + c^2*(c^2 - ab) ≥ 2*√[3*(a*b*c)^2] Therefore, the minimum value of a^4 + b^4 + c^4 - a^2*bc - b^2*ac - c^2*ab for positive numbers a, b, c is 2*√[3*(a*b*c)^2]. Now, summarize the answer above in one sentence, without any intermediate steps or explanations. The minimum value of the expression a^4 + b^4 + c^4 - a^2*bc - b^2*ac - c^2*ab for positive numbers a, b, c is 2*√[3*(a*b*c)^2].

Show that $a^4+b^4+c^4 \geq a+b+c$ The problem Let $a,b,c \in \mathbb{R}$ with $abc=1$. Show that $a^4+b^4+c^4 \geq a+b+c$ My idea We can write the inequality as $4a^4+4b^4+4c^4\geq 4a^2bc+ 4b^2ac+ 4c^2ab$ which is true by AM-GM ($2a^4+b^4+c^4 \geq 4a^2bc$) Is my idea right? I am in doubt because the numbers have to be real, and it doesn't specify if they are negative or positive. Because the question allows for all reals, your solution is likely worth $0^+$. It could depend on the strictness of the grader, but I believe that the phrasing is meant to catch those who blindly use AM-GM without accounting for the non-negative conditions. Your solution can be fixed by saying that $$ 2a^4 + b^4 + c^4 \geq 4|a^2bc| = 4|a| \geq 4a.$$ We satisfied the non-negative condition in AM-GM using the terms $a^2, b^2, c^2$. answered Dec 19, 2024 at 22:05 We need to show for all non-zero $a, b, c \in \mathbb R$, the inequality: $$a^4 + b^4 + c^4 ≥ a + b + c$$ holds true given that $abc = 1$. CASE 1: $a, b, c \in \mathbb R^+$ By the AM ≥ GM inequality (for positive reals): $$\dfrac{2a^4 + b^4 + c^4}{4} ≥ \sqrt{a^4(abc)^4} = a$$ Continuing this process for $b, c$ and then adding all the inequalities up will yield: $$\therefore a^4 + b^4 + c^4 ≥ a + b + c \longleftarrow \forall\ a, b, c \in \mathbb R^+$$ Note that equality will only hold when $a^4 = b^4 = c^4$ as per the AM ≥ GM inequality. Since this case deals with positive reals, $a = b = c = 1$ will result in equality because $a^4b^4c^4 = 1$. Case 2: $a, b, c \in \mathbb R$ Now, we include negative reals too. WLOG, suppose that $a a + b + c$$ Thus, we have shown in all cases that: $$\boxed{a^4 + b^4 + c^4 ≥ a + b + c}$$ where equality holds if and only if $a = b = c = 1$. $\blacksquare$ answered Dec 17, 2024 at 11:07 Here is a solution by using sum of squares $\geq 0$. Let y = x+1, so x = y-1.

$$1 - (y-1) + (y-1)^2 - (y-1)^3 + \cdots - (y-1)^9$$

**General term:** $(-1)^k (y-1)^k$ for $k = 0, 1, 2, \ldots, 9$

I need the coefficient of y² from $(-1)^k (y-1)^k$.

Using binomial expansion: $(y-1)^k = \sum_{j=0}^{k} \binom{k}{j} y^j (-1)^{k-j}$

The coefficient of y² is $\binom{k}{2}(-1)^{k-2} = \binom{k}{2}(-1)^{k-2}$ (only valid when k ≥ 2).

$$a_2 = \sum_{k=2}^{9} (-1)^k \binom{k}{2}(-1)^{k-2} = \sum_{k=2}^{9} \binom{k}{2}(-1)^{2k-2}$$

Since $2k-2$ is always even, $(-1)^{2k-2} = 1$.

$$a_2 = \sum_{k=2}^{9} \binom{k}{2} = \binom{10}{3} = 40$$

Hence

\[

\]

content.text:
Let me work through this.

Let \(S = (a+b)(a^4+b^4)-(a^2+b^2)(a^3+b^3)\).

Expand:
\[
(a+b)(a^4+b^4) = a^5 + ab^4 + a^4b + b^5
\]
\[
(a^2+b^2)(a^3+b^3) = a^5 + a^2b^3 + a^3b^2 + b^5
\]

Subtract:
\[
S = ab^4 + a^4b - a^2b^3 - a^3b^2
= ab(a^3 + b^3 - a^2b - ab^2)
\]

Factor \(a^3 + b^3 - a^2b - ab^2\):
\[
= a^3 - a^2b + b^3 - ab^2 = a^2(a-b) + b^2(b-a) = (a-b)(a^2 - b^2) = (a-b)^2(a+b)
\]

So
\[
S = ab(a-b)^2(a+b)
\]

Since \(a,b>0\), we have \(ab>0\), \(a+b>0\), and \((a-b)^2 \ge 0\). Thus \(S \ge 0\).

Equality when \(a=b\). Therefore the smallest value is \(0\).

content.content: Sophie Germain's Identity Cut-the-Knot｡An identity named after the famous french mathematician Sophie Germain (1776 - 1831) is a useful tool for math olympians: a4+4b4=(a2+2b2−2ab)(a2+2b2+2ab). The proof is by direct verification. Here's a problem that is easily solved with Sophie Germain's identity: Is 20154+42015 prime? Due to Sophie Germain's identity the answer is negative. Indeed, 20154+42015=20154+4⋅42014=20154+4⋅24028=20154+4⋅(21007)4=(20152+22015−2015⋅21008)(20152+22015+2015⋅21008). Since the second factor is clearly greater than 1, we only need to check that this is also true for the first factor. But 21007>211=2048>2015, implying that 22015>2015⋅21008. In fact, n4+4n, where n is a positive integer, is never a prime for n>1. It is even if n is even, and, if n is odd, we can simply generalize the above derivation. References A. Engel, Problem-Solving Strategies, Springer Verlag, 1998, p 121

For the pseudonymous identity used by Germain, see Antoine-Auguste Le Blanc. In mathematics, Sophie Germain's identity is a polynomial factorization named after Sophie Germain stating that x 4 + 4 y 4 = ( ( x + y ) 2 + y 2 ) ⋅ ( ( x − y ) 2 + y 2 ) = ( x 2 + 2 x y + 2 y 2 ) ⋅ ( x 2 − 2 x y + 2 y 2 ) . {\displaystyle {\begin{aligned}x^{4}+4y^{4}&={\bigl (}(x+y)^{2}+y^{2}{\bigr )}\cdot {\bigl (}(x-y)^{2}+y^{2}{\bigr )}\&=(x^{2}+2xy+2y^{2})\cdot (x^{2}-2xy+2y^{2}).\end{aligned}}} Beyond its use in elementary algebra, it can also be used in number theory to factorize integers of the special form x 4 + 4 y 4 {\displaystyle x^{4}+4y^{4}} , and it frequently forms the basis of problems in mathematics competitions. History Although the identity has been attributed to Sophie Germain, it does not appear in her works. Instead, in her works one can find the related identity x 4 + y 4 = ( x 2 − y 2 ) 2 + 2 ( x y ) 2 = ( x 2 + y 2 ) 2 − 2 ( x y ) 2 . {\displaystyle {\begin{aligned}x^{4}+y^{4}&=(x^{2}-y^{2})^{2}+2(xy)^{2}\&=(x^{2}+y^{2})^{2}-2(xy)^{2}.\\\end{aligned}}} Modifying this equation by multiplying y {\displaystyle y} by 2 {\displaystyle {\sqrt {2}}} gives x 4 + 4 y 4 = ( x 2 + 2 y 2 ) 2 − 4 ( x y ) 2 , {\displaystyle x^{4}+4y^{4}=(x^{2}+2y^{2})^{2}-4(xy)^{2},} a difference of two squares, from which Germain's identity follows. The inaccurate attribution of this identity to Germain was made by Leonard Eugene Dickson in his History of the Theory of Numbers, which also stated (equally inaccurately) that it could be found in a letter from Leonhard Euler to Christian Goldbach. The identity can be proven simply by multiplying the two terms of the factorization together, and verifying that their product equals the right hand side of the equality. A proof without words is also possible based on multiple applications of the Pythagorean theorem. Applications to integer factorization One consequence of Germain's identity is that the numbers of the form n 4 + 4 n {\displaystyle n^{4}+4^{n}} cannot be prime for n > 1 {\displaystyle n>1} . (For n = 1 {\displaystyle n=1} , the result is the prime number 5.) They are obviously not prime if n {\displaystyle n} is even, and if n {\displaystyle n} is odd they have a factorization given by the identity with x = n {\displaystyle x=n} and y = 2 ( n − 1 ) / 2 {\displaystyle y=2^{(n-1)/2}} . These numbers (starting with n = 0 {\displaystyle n=0} ) form the integer sequence 1, 5, 32, 145, 512, 1649, 5392, 18785, 69632, ... (sequence A001589 in the OEIS). Many of the appearances of Sophie Germain's identity in mathematics competitions come from this corollary of it.

content.title: Sophie Germain's identity
content.content: Sophie Germain's identity The On-Line Encyclopedia of Integer Sequences｡Sophie Germain's identity pertains to sums of fourth powers. Theorem. (Sophie Germain) Given real numbers x and y, x4+4y4=(x2−2xy+2y2)(x2+2xy+2y2). Proof. Rewrite x4+4y4 as (x2)2+(2y2)2+2x22y2−2x22y2, which can then be rewritten as (x2+2y2)2−(2xy)2 and finally (x2−2xy+2y2)(x2+2xy+2y2) as specified by the theorem. □ It may perhaps seem unnecessary to mention that the identity holds true if x or y or both are negative. Even-indexed powers of negative numbers are positive, so the left hand side of the equation is the same if we multiply xy or both by –1. If just one of them is negative, the right hand side changes subtly but without affecting the overall result: −2xy becomes a positive number but then 2xy becomes a negative number. For this reason we may safely ignore x, y value pairs containing negative numbers. Applications for results on prime numbers Theorem 5.1 The only prime number of the form x4+4y4 is 5. Proof. Assume x4+4y4 is prime. Sophie Germain's identity exposes two divisors of a number of this form, and since a prime number has only two distinct divisors, this must mean that x2+2xy+2y2=x4+4y4 and x2−2xy+2y2=1. Satisfying the latter equation is a necessary (but not sufficient) condition for the primality of x4+4y4. That equation has only four solutions, of which we will ignore the two solutions with negative numbers as they lead to the same results as their absolute values. This leaves x=1, y=0 and x=1, y=1. The former solution leads to x4+4y4=1, which is not prime, the latter to x4+4y4=5, which is prime. Since $1982 = 2 \cdot 991$, we compute mod 2 and mod 991.

Mod 2: $n$ ends in 2, so $n \equiv 0 \pmod 2$.

Mod 991: We need $2 \cdot \frac{10^{1980}-1}{9} \pmod{991}$. Note $9^{-1} \pmod{991}$. Since $9 \cdot 110 = 990 \equiv -1$, we have $9^{-1} \equiv -110 \equiv 881$.

So $n \equiv 2 \cdot 881 \cdot (10^{1980}-1) \pmod{991}$. Now $2 \cdot 881 = 1762 \equiv 771 \pmod{991}$.

We need $10^{1980} \pmod{991}$. By Fermat, $10^{990} \equiv 1 \pmod{991}$, and $1980 = 2 \cdot 990$, so $10^{1980} \equiv 1 \pmod{991}$.

Thus $n \equiv 771 \cdot (1 - 1) = 0 \pmod{991}$.

So $n \equiv 0$ mod both 2 and 991, hence $n \equiv 0 \pmod{1982}$.

Let me double check: $n = 2 \cdot \frac{10^{1980}-1}{9}$. Since $10^{1980} \equiv 1 \pmod{9 \cdot 991}$? Actually we have $10^{1980}-1$ divisible by 9 and by 991, so $\frac{10^{1980}-1}{9}$ divisible by 991. Then $n$ divisible by $2\cdot 991 = 1982$. Yes.

Solve the following problem. Make sure to show your work before giving the final answer. Find the minimum value of a^4+b^4+c^4-a^2*bc-b^2*ac-c^2*ab for positive numbers a, b, c. This problem can be solved using the AM-GM inequality (Arithmetic Mean-Geometric Mean Inequality). The AM-GM inequality states that the arithmetic mean of non-negative real numbers is greater than or equal to the geometric mean. In other words, if x1, x2, ..., xn are non-negative real numbers, then: (x1 + x2 + ... + xn) / n ≥ √[x1 * x2 * ... * xn] Let's apply this inequality to the given problem. We can rewrite the expression as follows: a^4 + b^4 + c^4 - a^2*bc - b^2*ac - c^2*ab = (a^4 - a^2*bc) + (b^4 - b^2*ac) + (c^4 - c^2*ab) = a^2*(a^2 - bc) + b^2*(b^2 - ac) + c^2*(c^2 - ab) Now, we apply the AM-GM inequality to each of the three terms: a^2*(a^2 - bc) ≥ 2*a*√[a^2*(a^2 - bc)] b^2*(b^2 - ac) ≥ 2*b*√[b^2*(b^2 - ac)] c^2*(c^2 - ab) ≥ 2*c*√[c^2*(c^2 - ab)] Adding these inequalities, we get: a^2*(a^2 - bc) + b^2*(b^2 - ac) + c^2*(c^2 - ab) ≥ 2*(a*√[a^2*(a^2 - bc)] + b*√[b^2*(b^2 - ac)] + c*√[c^2*(c^2 - ab)]) Now, we apply the AM-GM inequality again to the right side of the inequality: 2*(a*√[a^2*(a^2 - bc)] + b*√[b^2*(b^2 - ac)] + c*√[c^2*(c^2 - ab)]) ≥ 2*√[3*(a*b*c)^2] So, we have: a^2*(a^2 - bc) + b^2*(b^2 - ac) + c^2*(c^2 - ab) ≥ 2*√[3*(a*b*c)^2] Therefore, the minimum value of a^4 + b^4 + c^4 - a^2*bc - b^2*ac - c^2*ab for positive numbers a, b, c is 2*√[3*(a*b*c)^2]. Now, summarize the answer above in one sentence, without any intermediate steps or explanations. The minimum value of the expression a^4 + b^4 + c^4 - a^2*bc - b^2*ac - c^2*ab for positive numbers a, b, c is 2*√[3*(a*b*c)^2].

It could depend on the strictness of the grader, but I believe that the phrasing is meant to catch those who blindly use AM-GM without accounting for the non-negative conditions. Your solution can be fixed by saying that $$ 2a^4 + b^4 + c^4 \geq 4|a^2bc| = 4|a| \geq 4a.$$ We satisfied the non-negative condition in AM-GM using the terms $a^2, b^2, c^2$. answered Dec 19, 2024 at 22:05 We need to show for all non-zero $a, b, c \in \mathbb R$, the inequality: $$a^4 + b^4 + c^4 ≥ a + b + c$$ holds true given that $abc = 1$. CASE 1: $a, b, c \in \mathbb R^+$ By the AM ≥ GM inequality (for positive reals): $$\dfrac{2a^4 + b^4 + c^4}{4} ≥ \sqrt{a^4(abc)^4} = a$$ Continuing this process for $b, c$ and then adding all the inequalities up will yield: $$\therefore a^4 + b^4 + c^4 ≥ a + b + c \longleftarrow \forall\ a, b, c \in \mathbb R^+$$ Note that equality will only hold when $a^4 = b^4 = c^4$ as per the AM ≥ GM inequality. Since this case deals with positive reals, $a = b = c = 1$ will result in equality because $a^4b^4c^4 = 1$. Case 2: $a, b, c \in \mathbb R$ Now, we include negative reals too. WLOG, suppose that $a a + b + c$$ Thus, we have shown in all cases that: $$\boxed{a^4 + b^4 + c^4 ≥ a + b + c}$$ where equality holds if and only if $a = b = c = 1$. $\blacksquare$ answered Dec 17, 2024 at 11:07 Here is a solution by using sum of squares $\geq 0$. Homogenize the initial inequality to get $$a^4 + b^4 + c^4 \geq abc(a+b+c)$$ But is true for $a,b,c\in \mathbb R$ that $$(a^2-b^2)^2 + (b^2-c^2)^2 + (c^2-a^2)^2 + (ac-bc)^2 + (ab-ac)^2 + (bc-ab)^2\geq 0$$ which is equivalent to $2a^4 + 2b^4 + 2c^4 - 2a^2bc - 2b^2ac - 2c^2ab\geq 0$ which is the same as $a^4+b^4+c^4\geq abc(a+b+c)$.
